All 14 tests pass. Here's what each piece does and why it was designed this way:

**`ResultVisitor<T>` (new interface)**  
Two methods — `onDistances(Distances)` and `onNegativeCycle(NegativeCycle)` — one per concrete subtype. The generic `T` lets it serve both value-returning use cases (`String`, `int[]`, a UI model) and side-effect use cases (`Void`). The `of(Function, Function)` static factory avoids anonymous class boilerplate at call sites while keeping the interface itself simple.

**`ShortestPathResult`**  
Gains `<T> T accept(ResultVisitor<T> visitor)` — the only method it needs. Subtypes are now forced to implement dispatch correctly at compile time; a future third subtype would be a compile error until it also implements `accept`.

**`Distances` and `NegativeCycle`**  
Each implements `accept` with a single dispatch call to the matching visitor method. The dispatch is now in the type, not in the caller.

**`BellmanFordDemo`**  
The `if/else if (instanceof)` chain is gone. `accept` + `ResultVisitor.of` expresses the same two-case handling with the compiler enforcing exhaustiveness — if a third result type were ever added, all `accept` call sites would need updating, whereas the old `instanceof` chain would silently fall through.
